topStories.headline: SF Planning Formally Adopts Historic Survey for Haight Street and Cole Valley Commercial Districts
topStories.dek: The city's Historic Preservation Commission adopted Resolution R-1598 in June 2026, recognizing cultural resources along Haight Street, Cole Valley, and Divisadero Street — and neighborhood advocates are now mobilizing to expand the survey's reach.
topStories.body:
San Francisco's Planning Department has formally adopted survey findings for the Haight Street, Cole Valley, and Divisadero Street Neighborhood Commercial Districts, following a Historic Preservation Commission hearing on June 3, 2026, at which Resolution R-1598 was passed. The survey is part of the SF Survey, the city's ongoing Citywide Cultural Resources Survey program, which identifies and documents places of cultural, historical, and architectural importance across San Francisco's diverse communities.

The adopted findings follow a 2024 milestone when SF Planning approved the Citywide Historic Context Statement for Counterculture (1965–1975), which identifies significant locations tied to the Summer of Love era and related movements. While the counterculture context statement covers many specific Haight sites, the Haight Ashbury Neighborhood Council (HANC) noted in early July that those locations have not yet been fully indexed within the document, and that neighborhood history extends well beyond the 1965–1975 window.

At its July 9 meeting, HANC President Richard Ivanhoe called on community members to help identify historic treasures within HANC's borders — from Arguello to Divisadero and from Fulton to 17th Street. The current SF Survey is focused on Haight Street from Central to Shrader, and HANC is working to build on the city's official findings by documenting the last block of Haight Street between Shrader and Stanyan, an area not yet covered by the formal survey.

Residents interested in contributing to the neighborhood's historic record can download the adopted survey findings and counterculture context statement from the SF Planning website at sfplanning.org, or attend upcoming HANC meetings held on the second Thursday of each month at 7 p.m. at the Park Branch Library, 1833 Page Street.

topStories.headline: Muni Approves $1.5B Budget to Avert Immediate Cuts, But Long-Term Funding Crisis Looms
topStories.dek: The SFMTA board unanimously passed a two-year budget closing a $307 million shortfall for fiscal year 2026–27 — but transit officials warn that without new ballot-measure revenue, the system could face the elimination of up to 20 Muni lines.
topStories.body:
The San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA) Board of Directors unanimously approved a balanced two-year operating budget of $1.5 billion for fiscal year 2026–27 and $1.6 billion for FY 2027–28, closing an immediate shortfall of $307 million in the first year beginning July 1, 2026. For Haight and Cole Valley residents who depend on the 7-Haight/Noriega, 33-Ashbury, 6-Parnassus, and N-Judah lines, the approved budget preserves current Muni and paratransit service for the coming two fiscal years.

The agency described the crisis as the largest budget deficit in its history, driven by the expiration of one-time pandemic relief funding, declining parking and fare revenue, and costs that have continued to rise with inflation. Muni ridership has improved since the pandemic but remains about 25 percent below pre-pandemic peaks, further straining the agency's finances.

To close the gap, the budget relies on three revenue strategies: internal cost savings and efficiency measures, a regional ballot measure known as the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative proposing a half-cent sales tax across multiple counties, and a local Stronger Muni for All ballot measure. SFMTA officials have warned that if voters reject these measures in a future election, the agency could be forced to cut up to one-third of Muni service, eliminate up to 20 routes, shorten service hours, and reduce cable car and F-Market streetcar operations.

The approved budget also includes a two-year capital budget of $655 million in the first year and $546 million in the second, focused on sustaining Muni infrastructure, vehicles, and technology. The structural deficit is still projected to grow to $434 million by 2030 without new permanent funding sources.

topStories.headline: Cole Valley and Haight Housing Prices Heat Up in Competitive Q2 2026 Market
topStories.dek: Homes in Cole Valley and the Haight are selling well above asking price amid citywide competition fueled in part by AI-sector wealth, according to a Q2 2026 San Francisco real estate market report.
topStories.body:
San Francisco's housing market saw intensifying competition in the second quarter of 2026, and the Haight and Cole Valley area was no exception. According to a Q2 2026 market report drawing on Vanguard Properties data, Cole Valley and Haight homes sold for an average of more than 136 percent of asking price — one of the highest sale-to-list ratios in the city and on par with the red-hot Sunset district.

The market data for Cole Valley specifically reflects a tight-inventory environment. A March 2026 snapshot showed a median sale price of $2,275,000, with homes going pending in just 11 days and a sale-to-list ratio of approximately 116 percent. A separate April 2026 analysis of apartment buildings in the Noe, Eureka, and Cole Valleys district found a median investment property price of approximately $2.5 million.

Real estate analysts have linked part of the surge in competition citywide to wealth generated by San Francisco's expanding artificial intelligence sector, though the effect is not evenly distributed across neighborhoods and property types. In Lower Haight, average condo sale times compressed dramatically, with units selling in roughly 14 days as of spring 2026 — a nearly 46-percent acceleration compared with the prior year — and inventory across the city continued to tighten as homeowners with low locked-in mortgage rates declined to sell.

For renters and prospective first-time buyers in the Haight and Cole Valley, the competitive conditions underscore ongoing affordability pressures in an already premium market.
topStories.sourceName: Mark D McHale & Associates / Vanguard Properties Q2 2026

events.title: Counterculture Museum — Ongoing Exhibitions
events.location: Counterculture Museum, 1485 Haight St. (at Ashbury), Haight-Ashbury
events.description: The Counterculture Museum, which opened in May 2025 at the historic corner of Haight and Ashbury and was named one of TIME's World's Greatest Places in 2026, presents immersive exhibits on the 1960s counterculture, the Summer of Love, civil rights, women's liberation, and LGBTQ+ rights. General admission $10; reduced rate $8 for students, seniors, teachers, and military.

moreNews.headline: Counterculture Museum Celebrates First Anniversary and Allen Ginsberg Centennial
moreNews.body: The Counterculture Museum at 1485 Haight Street — which opened in May 2025 at the exact corner of Haight and Ashbury and was recognized by TIME magazine as one of the World's Greatest Places in 2026 — recently concluded a weeklong series of events celebrating its first anniversary and the centennial of poet Allen Ginsberg. The museum, run by Jerry and Estelle Cimino (founders of the Beat Museum in North Beach), covers the psychedelic movement, the Summer of Love, anti-war activism, women's liberation, LGBTQ+ rights, and the Black Panthers, and includes a small stage for readings and live events. The museum is open Wednesday through Sunday, 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., with general admission at $10.

moreNews.headline: HANC July Meeting Recap: Neighborhood Weighs In on Two Park Projects
moreNews.body: According to the Haight Ashbury Neighborhood Council's website, the July meeting centered on two park-related projects affecting the neighborhood, following a June session in which political analyst Calvin Welch reviewed the June 2026 primary election results and how the Haight-Ashbury and adjacent precincts voted. The analysis covered 12 precincts across three supervisorial districts, noting that North Panhandle precincts tend to cast a liberal vote, Flatland precincts lean left-progressive, and the hillside precincts vote more moderately. Voter turnout was the third lowest for a primary election in the past decade. HANC meets on the second Thursday of each month at 7 p.m. at the Park Branch Library, 1833 Page Street.

moreNews.headline: Muni's Ballot Funding Measures Will Shape Service on Haight-Area Lines This Fall
moreNews.body: Haight-Ashbury, Lower Haight, Cole Valley, and Panhandle residents who rely on Muni lines 7, 33, 6, and the N-Judah will be watching closely as two critical transit funding measures head toward a future ballot. The SFMTA's approved FY2026–27 budget staves off immediate service cuts, but officials warn that without passage of the Connect Bay Area Transit Initiative (a regional half-cent sales tax) and the local Stronger Muni for All parcel tax, the agency's structural deficit is projected to grow to $434 million by 2030 — potentially forcing elimination of up to 20 Muni lines and other dramatic service reductions. Residents can follow SFMTA budget updates at sfmta.com.
